en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 55, the Jīvakasutta. Thus have I heard: [the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove.]
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove.

Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said this to the Blessed One:
“I have heard this, Bhante:”
“They slaughter living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama; knowing this, the ascetic Gotama knowingly consumes meat prepared specifically for him, as a result of that action.
Venerable sir, as for those who say this: “They slaughter living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama;
knowing this, the ascetic Gotama knowingly consumes meat prepared specifically for him, as a result of that action”—do they speak truthfully of the Blessed One?

“Do they speak what has been said, and do they not misrepresent the Blessed One with falsehood, but explain in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no legitimate criticism can be reasonably leveled against them?
“Jīvaka, those who say: ‘They slaughter living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama; the ascetic [Gotama]...’”
"Gotama eats meat that has been specifically prepared for him and is dependent upon that action"—those who say this do not speak my words;
they misrepresent me with what is untrue and non-factual.
Jīvaka, I say that there are three grounds on which meat is not to be consumed.
"Jīvaka, I say that meat is not to be consumed for three reasons: what has been seen, what has been heard, and what is suspected.
Jīvaka, I say that meat is to be consumed for three reasons."
"Jīvaka, I say that meat may be consumed for three reasons: when it has not been seen, heard, or suspected [to have been killed for one's sake].
Here, Jīvaka, a bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town."
Thus, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwells pervading one quarter; likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Then a householder or a householder’s son approaches him and invites him for a meal on the following day.
If he so desires, Jīvaka, the bhikkhu accepts.
At the end of that night, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he goes to where that [householder]...
He approaches the residence of a householder or a householder’s son; having approached, he sits down on a prepared seat.
Then that householder or householder’s son serves him with excellent almsfood.
It does not occur to him:
‘It would be good indeed if this householder or householder’s son were to serve me with choice almsfood.
Or: ‘Oh, may this householder or householder’s son continue to serve me with such choice almsfood in the future!’—such thoughts do not occur to him.
Thus, he consumes that almsfood unattached, uninfatuated, and uninfused with craving, seeing the danger in it and possessing the wisdom of escape.
What do you think, Jīvaka,
would that bhikkhu at that time intend for his own affliction, or intend for the affliction of another, or intend for the affliction of both?”
“No, venerable sir.
“In that case, Jīvaka, does not that bhikkhu at that time consume only blameless food?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
"I have heard this, Bhante:
'Brahmā dwells in loving-kindness.
This, Bhante, has been personally witnessed by me in the Blessed One."
“Indeed, Bhante, the Blessed One dwells in loving-kindness.

“Jīvaka, as for the lust, the hatred, and the delusion by which one would be full of ill will—those lust, those hatred, and those delusions have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and subject to non-arising in the future.
If you spoke this with reference to that, Jīvaka, I grant you this.”
“Indeed, Bhante, it was with reference to this very point that I spoke.
“In this case, Jīvaka, a bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town.
With a mind imbued with compassion... [and so on]...”
With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy …pe… with a mind accompanied by equanimity,
he dwells pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across,
everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity— vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
A householder or a householder’s son approaches him and invites him for a meal on the following day.
If he so desires, Jīvaka, the bhikkhu accepts.

At the end of that night, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he goes to the residence of that householder or householder’s son; having arrived, he sits down on the prepared seat.
Then that householder or householder’s son serves him with excellent almsfood.
It does not occur to him:
“It would be good indeed if this householder or householder’s son were to serve me with excellent almsfood.”
‘Oh, that this householder or householder’s son might continue to serve me with such excellent almsfood in the future!’—
such a thought does not occur to him.
He consumes that almsfood unattached, uninfatuated, and uninfused with craving, seeing the danger in it and possessing wisdom regarding the escape from it.
“What do you think, Jīvaka,
would that bhikkhu at that time intend for his own affliction, or intend for the affliction of another, or intend for the affliction of both?
“No, indeed, Bhante.”
“But, Jīvaka, does that bhikkhu at that time not consume only blameless food?
“Yes, venerable sir.
I have heard this, venerable sir:”
‘Brahmā dwells in equanimity.
This, venerable sir, has been personally witnessed by me;
for the Blessed One, venerable sir, dwells in equanimity.”
“Jīvaka, whatever lust, hatred, or delusion by which one might be subject to violence, discontent, or aversion— such lust, such hatred,
and such delusion have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and are of a nature not to arise again in the future.”
“If, Jīvaka, you spoke this with reference to that, I grant you this.
“Indeed, Bhante, it was precisely with reference to that that I spoke.
“Jīvaka, whoever slaughters a living being for the sake of the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata produces much demerit on five grounds.”
Furthermore, householder, when he says, “Go,
bring such-and-such a living being,” by this first ground he generates much demerit. Furthermore,
when that living being experiences pain and mental distress while being brought along with its neck bound in a halter, by this second ground he generates much demerit.
When he says, “Go,
kill this living being,” by this third ground he generates much demerit. When that living being,
being killed, experiences pain and mental distress, by this fourth ground he generates much demerit.
“Furthermore, Jīvaka, when one offends a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata with what is improper, by this fifth ground one generates much demerit.
Whoever, Jīvaka, slaughters a living being for the sake of a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata, generates much demerit by these five grounds.
When this was said, Jīvaka Komārabhacca addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!
Truly, venerable sir, the bhikkhus consume their food in a way that is permissible;
truly, venerable sir, the bhikkhus consume their food in a way that is blameless.”
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante!
… [as above] … May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
The Jīvakasutta, the fifth, is concluded.
